articles.title: Building Software for Pet Care: What Developers Should Consider Beyond CRUD
articles.excerpt: When developers think about business software, the first things that often come to mind are familiar patterns: users, products, orders, dashboards, authentication, and CRUD operations. Pet-care softwa…
articles.body: When developers think about business software, the first things that often come to mind are familiar patterns: users, products, orders, dashboards, authentication, and CRUD operations. Pet-care software looks simple at first. A boarding business needs to store pets, owners, reservations, and payments. But once you look closely at the workflow, the domain becomes considerably more interesting. A pet is not simply another database record. A reservation is not simply another calendar event. And a boarding facility is not simply another business dashboard. Building software for pet-care businesses requires developers to think about relationships, scheduling, operational workflows, permissions, automation, and the real-world behavior of the people using the system.

articles.title: Migrate Jira users and groups without escalation
articles.excerpt: When you migrate Jira users and groups to a Cloud site that already has a group with the same name, the two are not kept apart. They are joined by name, and everyone in the source group ends up inheri…
articles.body: When you migrate Jira users and groups to a Cloud site that already has a group with the same name, the two are not kept apart. They are joined by name, and everyone in the source group ends up inheriting whatever the Cloud group can do. Atlassian says it plainly on its own page, "How Jira users and groups are migrated": "Group linking is identified by group name and could result in permission escalation during migration. Make sure you check your groups before migrating." That sentence is easy to scroll past. It is also the reason the Jira pre-migration checklist has one item marked mandatory that has nothing to do with data: "Check for conflicts with group names".
articles.author: Mihai Perdum

articles.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Message Format Explained
articles.excerpt: Short answer: The Model Context Protocol message format is JSON-RPC 2.0 — one request object jsonrpc, method, params, and an id, one result or error object back, and notifications id at all. Over HTTP…
articles.body: Short answer: The Model Context Protocol message format is JSON-RPC 2.0 — one request object with jsonrpc , method , params , and an id , one result or error object back, and notifications that carry no id at all. Over HTTP the whole conversation is POSTed to a single endpoint: initialize , then tools/list , then tools/call , with the session optional. The parts that break integrations are the small ones: an empty params array, an arguments field typed as a list, and a client that calls the tool name as the method. Key takeaways Three shapes, one envelope. Requests ( id + method + params ), notifications (no id ), and results ( id + result or error ) — every MCP message is one of them. initialize is a negotiation, not a formality.

articles.title: Data privacy isn’t just for nerds — here’s why you should care too
articles.excerpt: The more I see how my personal data is used across services, the more I want to guard my privacy.
articles.body: A lot of times when I’ve mentioned moving to more privacy-focused apps and services, the reaction is more than a shrug — it’s a declaration that online privacy isn’t all that important. Most recently, at a tech event, I mentioned moving to Brave to avoid Google’s data collection and targeted advertising, and another attendee said that it’s just not important to them. That’s when I realized that there’s this general misunderstanding that prioritizing data privacy is the pastime of nerds and those prone to donning tin foil hats. I know I was someone who used to take a more laissez-faire approach to my online privacy. Years later, after grappling with the consequences of this, I feel that data privacy and data collection should be something everyone cares about.

articles.body: As soon as I picked up the Google Pixel 11 for the first time, I knew I wanted to love it. The slimmer, all-glass camera bar spoke to me as the perfect blend between the Pixel 10a’s flat back and the Pixel 11 Pro’s thicker camera housing. My favorite Android 17 perks, like the Pixel-exclusive Magic Capture and Creator Suite, still made the cut for Google’s cheapest flagship. And the missing features aren’t significant enough to notice they’re gone on the $899 Pixel 11. Unfortunately, after actually getting my hands on one, I found the Pixel 11 hard to love. Eventually, Marvel greenlit Daredevil: Born Again , which was supposed to be an all-new continuity with the characters, albeit with some of the same cast. articles.title: 70 Years Later, The Greatest Closing Line In Fantasy History Is Still The Wisest Book Quote Of The 1950s
articles.excerpt: Why the quiet simplicity of Tolkien's ending remains fantasy's best
articles.body: The fantasy genre is built on unforgettable final acts that leave the stage in a blaze of spectacle. George R.R. Martin famously closes A Game of Thrones by spectacularly reawakening magic with the birth of dragons, while Brandon Sanderson caps the Mistborn trilogy with a universe-altering revelation of godhood. Others lean into existential weight, trapping readers in inescapable loops, much like Stephen King did with The Dark Tower or the metafictional continuity of Andrzej Sapkowski’s The Witcher . These are undeniably some of the greatest closing notes in literature (fantasy or otherwise), designed to leave audiences in awe of the cosmic and mythic scale of the worlds they inhabited.

articles.body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley in March 2026 demonstrated autonomous technology that could identify an incursion – a vehicle, wayward suitcase, or other runway obstacle that could impact an aircraft’s safe landing. NASA/Brandon Torres-Navarrete NASA’s researchers know that when you settle into your seat on a commercial flight, you expect a smooth takeoff, views over the clouds, a steady descent, and hopefully an early arrival at your destination. But when your flight gets delayed on the tarmac instead of lifting off, or it ends up in a holding pattern rather than landing on time, things start to change.

articles.title: NASA Selects Far-Infrared Telescope as First in New Mission Class
articles.excerpt: NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space…
articles.body: Credit: NASA NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space telescope is the first in a new class of NASA astrophysics missions, called Probe Explorers, within the agency’s longstanding Explorers Program. “The PRIMA mission is humanity’s next window into the deep universe. It will unveil the obscure across cosmic time to better understand the formation of planets, stars, black holes, and even how water on Earth came to be,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington.

articles.title: NASA Aircraft to Make Low-Altitude Research Flights Over Colorado
articles.excerpt: Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammoni…
articles.body: A photo of the Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft, which will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Greeley, Colorado, to measure emissions in October 2026. Dynamic Aviation Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from agricultural lands and animal farms and the interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University.  The Colorado deployment is the first series of flights for the FarmFlux mission.
